title: Electoral Legislation Amendment (Electoral Funding and Disclosure Reform) Bill 2018
short_title: Electoral Legislation Amendment (Electoral Funding and Disclosure Reform) Bill 2018

summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: The bill would tighten the rules on political donations and spending in federal elections.

It would create a new Transparency Register, require large political spenders to report to the Australian Electoral Commission, and ban gifts over $100 from foreign donors intended for election campaigning.
Gifts between $1,000 and the disclosure threshold from key political actors would need a donor certificate that they are not foreign, and gifts above that threshold would require donor verification.
changes: Establishes a Transparency Register as a central repository for information disclosed under Part XX of the Electoral Act.
Requires those with high electoral expenditure to register with the Australian Electoral Commission and follow similar disclosure rules as political parties.
Clarifies the definition of electoral expenditure in Part XX of the Electoral Act.
Requires discretionary government benefits to be reported under the current financial disclosure scheme.
Prohibits giving and knowingly receiving gifts over $100 from foreign donors if the donor intends the gift to be used for electoral expenditure.
Limits public election funding to demonstrated electoral spending.
summary.affected: Political parties, political campaigners, donors, and key political actors.

speeches.speaker: Alex Hawke
speeches.brief: The bill introduces registration and disclosure obligations for third-party campaigners, creates a new "political campaigner" category for those spending over $100,000 annually, bans foreign donations over $250 to parties, candidates, and significant campaigners, and limits public funding to demonstrated electoral spending.

speeches.speaker: Andrew Leigh
speeches.brief: Labor supports the final Electoral Legislation Amendment Bill banning foreign donations, but criticises the government's original draft as poorly drafted and threatening to charities; Labor has voluntarily refused foreign donations for over a year and calls on the Liberal and National parties to immediately stop taking foreign donations from donors like Lord Ashcroft and Peter Briger, and commits to lowering the disclosure threshold to $1,000 if it forms government.

speeches.speaker: Andrew Giles
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the Electoral Legislation Amendment (Electoral Funding and Disclosure Reform) Bill 2018 as a step toward banning foreign donations and restoring trust in politics, urging conservative parties to adopt its principles immediately. He credited amendments from the Joint Standing Committee on Electoral Matters, civil society groups like the Hands Off Our Charities alliance, and contributions from Senator Reynolds, Senator Lee Rhiannon, Senator Farrell, and Senator Cormann.

speeches.speaker: Luke Gosling
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that Labor has long supported banning foreign donations, including a 2016 election policy and a Senate bill, while the government's initial legislation was flawed and united charities against it. Labor voluntarily refused foreign donations and worked with the Joint Standing Committee on Electoral Matters—including the member for Scullin, member for Oxley, and Senators Ketter and Brown—to make the bill more workable.

speeches.speaker: Rebekha Sharkie
speeches.brief: The speaker argued for a $1,000 donation limit for all donors, real-time disclosure, and monthly reporting of gifts and loans within 10 days, criticising Labor for not pursuing these measures and calling for a model similar to Canada's to reduce the influence of big money in politics.
